articles.sourceTitle: U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
articles.title: U.S. closes loophole allowing remote access to AI chips : NPR
articles.text:
U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout

Data center company Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026. The company is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies. A new Commerce Department rule would restrict that access.

Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images

hide caption

Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images

The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.

The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.   Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.

The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.   The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security   However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.   "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.   The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.   Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.

Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.   "Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.   In a joint statement late Monday, the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice said that U.S. authorities had launched a criminal investigation into Megaspeed in 2025 after conducting an "on-site, in-person, end-use check" at the Singaporean-based company and interviewing its then CEO Alice Huang.   "Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation against Megaspeed," the statement said.   In the statement posted on X, the two departments said they "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."    The statement also provided a timeline of the ongoing probe against Megaspeed, detailing how the investigation was initiated in 2024 by the Department of Commerce "for potential export control violations" after "identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion." It said that the probe involved a request to Nvidia to provide records of "direct or indirect sales" to the company. According to the statement, by June 2025 Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on their "no sell" list.   Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.   The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."   Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.

The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.   "We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.

How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
articles.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
articles.text:
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.
Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.
That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.
What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.
You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.
So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.
NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN
No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.
If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes.
Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.
E2E tests
If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.
The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you what’s broken.
FIG AA unit test may show “Error: Timeout after 30 seconds,” but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of what’s broken.
While unit tests are faster and less flaky, it’s possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test don’t understand the full task.
With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like CDP, simulators, or API harnesses.
The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the user’s point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.
Property tests: constraints that can’t break
A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.
You start by writing a statement you think can’t fail and then use a test library (fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.
There are many properties in virtually every software project like:

Round-trip encoding: “if you encode X then decode it back, you get X.” This works for parsing and serialization as well.
Invariants: Things that must always be true, like “account balance can never become negative.”
Idempotency: Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once.
Equivalence: Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code.

Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that aren’t created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.
Differential tests: the old system is the oracle
Differential tests are particularly effective for large-scale migration use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.
The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. You’ll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.
HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION
We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.
Verification means running the change
Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.
Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.
To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.
Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.
When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.
Failing tests require human attention
Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.
Code owners write their own checks
The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.
Reliability checks trigger on the diff
We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is “--resume loads old transcripts.” When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won’t have it.
Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches–usually 3 to 10–so nobody has to memorize past outages.
One reviewer, multiple rounds
We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.
We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It’s cheaper and finds more.
Changes can't modify their own checks
If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.
The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.
The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite.
Start a new gate in observe mode
In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.
We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.
Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.
Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck – Claude Code isn't perfect.
Test your checks on what actually matters
The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.
This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.
They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.
In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.
Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing. The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.
Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.
Turn misses into rules
In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.
The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.
Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them,

articles.sourceTitle: Regulatory Capture by Anthropic Through METR
articles.title: Kevin Bass (@kevinnbass): "I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances. What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation. Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture. It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off. Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle. It starts with METR. Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models. He proposes METR for this purpose. But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock. Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio. And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem. This stock was worth $500 million early last year. It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later. METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth. Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well. But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much. The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all. The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll. If this were the end of it, that's bad. But that isn't all. The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom. The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others. They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's. All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile. As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder. Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created. From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts. This itself is an objective fact. The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it. But the problem also goes in the other direction: If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die. Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen. Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly. They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic. And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly. What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations. The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture. And that feedback loop is winning. That's what Jacob Coxon is. China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China. America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level. Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences. Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully. It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America. Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear. Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers. Congress must investigate. Evidence and Github in next post. Then some supplementary figures."
articles.text: == Anthropic equity, the donated stake, and the accounts that pay Coefficient's grants == Claim: Anthropic's Series H release (May 28 2026) names Jane Street and D.E. Shaw Ventures among the investors; individual amounts are not disclosed. Why it matters: Fixes the Series H investor list that the panel and the $965B valuation rest on, and shows the firm-level Jane Street link to the lab whose staff METR names as donors. Source: anthropic.com/news/series-h Claim: Forbes (Nov 7 2025, Phoebe Liu) put the Moskovitz–Tuna Anthropic stake at "an estimated $500 million". Why it matters: The only published dollar estimate of the donated stake; it is the left bar of the chart and the '$500M' in the title. Source: forbes.com.au/news/billionai… Claim: Forbes, quoting Cari Tuna: the stake "was moved into a nonprofit vehicle in early 2025" to "dispel any perception of conflict of interest". The vehicle is not named. Why it matters: Establishes that the stake was donated in early 2025 and that Tuna gave conflict-of-interest as the reason; the vehicle is unnamed, which is the question the rest of the stakes rows try to close. Source: forbes.com.au/news/billionai… Claim: Jaan Tallinn told Postimees (Feb 2026) that he is an Anthropic board observer rather than a director. Why it matters: Tallinn, METR's other large early funder through SFF, is an Anthropic board observer by his own account; the figure says 'observer', never 'director'. Source: majandus.postimees.ee/841860… Claim: Forbes reports that Eric Schmidt's family office, Hillspire, bought 20% of D.E. Shaw & Co.; Schmidt's Forbes profile does not mention Anthropic. Why it matters: Links Schmidt, a Series A investor and METR supporter through Schmidt Sciences, to D.E. Shaw, whose venture arm joined Series H; the figure uses Forbes' exact 20%. Source: forbes.com/profile/eric-schm… Claim: Anthropic's Series A release names the Center for Emerging Risk Research (now Macroscopic Ventures) as an investor; its Series B release names it again. Amounts undisclosed. Why it matters: CERR/Macroscopic is both an Anthropic Series A and B investor and a funder of Redwood and Longview, two of METR's intermediaries. Source: anthropic.com/news/anthropic… Claim: Dustin Moskovitz (Good Ventures Foundation, EIN 46-1008520) — no private-stock contribution in FY2025 (Jul 2024–Jun 2025): Schedule B lists one non-cash gift, publicly traded securities, $1,395,695,354, received 2025-06-30, from the Dustin A Moskovitz Remainder Interest Trust; plus $150,027 from Beneficial AI Foundation USD (2025-06-30, IRS 990-PF filing) Why it matters: Good Ventures Foundation's own FY2025 Schedule B lists two contributors and one non-cash gift of publicly traded securities; no private stock. So the shares had not reached the 990-PF filer by June 2025. Source: apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/9… Claim: Dustin Moskovitz (Good Ventures Foundation, EIN 46-1008520) — no Anthropic holding named: corporate-stock schedule lists 406 public issuers (3i Group … Alphabet Class A $125.5M …); other investments only by category (private equity $1,339,422,459; venture capital $259,560,574; SAFE agreements $7,500,000; hedge funds $906,041,941; private credit $658,286,371; real assets $410,252,102; fixed income $322,362,362) USD (2025-06-30, IRS 990-PF filing) Why it matters: The foundation's investment schedules name 406 public issuers and no Anthropic holding; indirect exposure through funds cannot be excluded. Source: apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/9… Claim: Alexander Berger (CEO, Coefficient Giving), on X — "He's since donated his stake (and not to us)" (2025-12-18, self-statement) Why it matters: Coefficient's CEO says the stake was donated and 'not to us', so Coefficient's own entities are out; the recipient is still unnamed. Source: nitter.cf/albrgr/status/20016699… Claim: Dustin Moskovitz, on Bluesky (@moskov.goodventures.org) — "GV is itself a beneficiary of that wave (via Anthropic and a number of other investments)" (2026-08-26, self-statement) Why it matters: Moskovitz says Good Ventures is 'itself a beneficiary' of the coming wave of AI wealth 'via Anthropic', i.e. the giving complex expects to gain when Anthropic gains. Source: bsky.app/profile/moskov.good… Claim: Forbes (Phoebe Liu), US original — the couple give through Good Ventures Foundation "plus more in donor-advised funds"; the foundation's largest holdings do not include Anthropic (2025-11-07, press) Why it matters: Forbes says the couple give through Good Ventures Foundation 'plus more in donor-advised funds', which is why the DAF route is on the figure. Source: forbes.com/sites/phoebeliu/2… Claim: Dustin Moskovitz (Forbes "True Net Worth" reranking, Matt Durot and Chase Peterson-Withorn) — less than 0.8 (donated "last year") % (Forbes estimate) (2026-04-20, Forbes-Bloomberg estimate) Why it matters: Forbes' 'less than 0.8%' is the only percentage bound found; 0.8% of the $965B Series H valuation is the $7.7B ceiling on the figure. Source: forbes.com/sites/mattdurot/2… Claim: Dustin Moskovitz, on Bluesky (@moskov.goodventures.org) — "We fund people like METR and Redwood who have been the ones writing the reports on the agent swarms" (2026-09-11, self-statement) Why it matters: Moskovitz's own words that his giving funds METR and Redwood. Source: bsky.app/profile/moskov.good… Claim: Full-text scan of every IRS e-file batch received in 2025 and 2026 for the word "Anthropic" (scripts/irs_anthropic_scan.sh) — no return names a Moskovitz/Tuna entity holding Anthropic; eleven returns mention Anthropic at all: as a vendor or training partner (five 990-EZ/990 filers); Alignment Research Center 2024 990 (program text on the evals spin-out); and four private foundations holding or receiving it: The Laniakea Charitable Foundation (EIN 85-4307164, Milwaukee, FYE 2024-11-30: "ANTHROPIC SPV" $190,872 beside "SITUATIONAL AWARENESS FUND" $20,000,000), Bright Moon Foundation (87-3664806, Bellevue WA: "INVESTMENT-ANTHROPIC" $150,000 in 2024 and 2025 returns), The Nathan Cummings Foundation (23-7093201, New York: "ANTHROPIC, PBC" $1,869,251 among other investments), Commoncrawl Foundation (26-1635908: "Anthropic PBC" as a $250,000 contributor) (2026-09-14, IRS TEOS bulk e-files (index_2025.csv, index_2026.csv; 2025 batches 01–12, 2026 batches 01–07, A–D halves; ≈900,000 returns)) Why it matters: A full-text scan of every IRS e-file received in 2025 and 2026 finds no return naming Anthropic stock held by a Moskovitz or Tuna vehicle; a bounded negative. Source: apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/9… Claim: Dustin Moskovitz Remainder Interest Trust dated March 10, 2018 (identity, from Meta's 2020 proxy) — the trust that supplies Good Ventures Foundation's largest gifts is identified: trustee Tom Van Loben Sels (also Good Ventures Foundation's assistant secretary and the officer on Coefficient Giving Policy Fund's 990-N); it held 6,830,855 Meta Class B shares in March 2020, the same block earlier held by "The Dustin Moskovitz 2008 Annuity Trust dated March 10, 2008" (Meta 2015 proxy), i.e. the remainder of a ten-year 2008 GRAT; Moskovitz is "trustee, co-trustee, grantor, or beneficiary" shares (2020-04-10, SEC DEF 14A (Facebook, Inc. 2020 proxy, footnote 17; 2015 proxy footnote)) Why it matters: Identifies the family trust that makes the foundation's largest gifts; its holdings are on no public document. Source: sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… Claim: Anthropic investor base (NYT, Mike Isaac et al., Sep 3 2026, corrected Sep 4) — no figure for any METR-named funder; "Menlo, Lightspeed and Iconiq now own 1 percent to 2 percent of Anthropic, said three people"; "Anthropic has raised more than $130 billion from roughly 300 investors, according to PitchBook"; "Spark Capital is the only investor with a seat on Anthropic's board" % (2026-09-03, press) Why it matters: The NYT's investor-base reporting gives no percentage for any METR-named funder; nothing in the press resolves the stake. Source: nytimes.com/2026/09/03/techn… Claim: Jane Street (WSJ, Jun 20 2026, "Secretive Wall Street Powerhouse Jane Street Seizes the AI Spotlight") — no share count or value for the Anthropic stake; the piece says Jane Street's profits were "helped in part by gains from investments in Anthropic and other private companies" and that its private-investment figure "includes a stake in Anthropic that was purchased in 2024 from the estate of FTX" (2026-06-20, press) Why it matters: The WSJ confirms Jane Street's Anthropic position came partly from the FTX estate sale but gives no current share count. Source: wsj.com/tech/ai/jane-street-… Claim: Jaan Tallinn (Äripäev "aasta ettevõtja" profile, Jan 5 2026) — declines to state a percentage: "Meil on väike majapidamine, tiitleid ei kasuta ja protsente ei kuuluta" (We have a small household, we do not use titles and we do not announce percentages); "Äripäevaga suhelnud inimesed oletavad, et portfell on väärt miljardeid" (people who spoke to Äripäev assume the portfolio is worth billions); Metaplanet's investments are run by Rauno Miljand; Anthropic "now worth about $350 billion" (2026-01-05, press (Estonian)) Why it matters: Tallinn declines to state his Anthropic percentage, so his dashed link is 'undisclosed'. articles.title: I Went to a Caltech Math Class Where AI Upended Homework
articles.text:
I went to a math class at Caltech. The professor no longer grades homework because everyone's using AI.

Truman Dickerson

I went to a math class at Caltech, where the specter of AI loomed large.

This story is available exclusively to Business Insider
subscribers. Become an Insider
and start reading now.
Have an account? .

Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday.Though the instruction was entirely analog, the specter of AI loomed large.Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told me that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion."There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI."Chatbots, once derided for their inability to perform such basic tasks as counting the r's in "strawberry," can now do math as well as a graduate student.And if you're an undergraduate student, that's kind of a big deal. Some, Business Insider has reported, are reconsidering whether to study math at all.From my perch near the back of the lecture hall on Friday, however, I didn't see any students prompting ChatGPT.In many ways, the class resembled a typical early morning university lecture (for undergrads, 10 a.m. is basically the crack of dawn). Sweatshirted students arrived late and filtered in the upper rows, while the overachievers sat in the front and asked questions.Many bent their heads over large iPads and took furious notes while Yi filled up blackboard after blackboard with formulas and practice problems. Some had no note-taking materials to speak of. A couple closed their eyes for extended periods.

Want more Business Insider in your news feed?

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

The class is a "core requirement" in Caltech's curriculum, meaning everyone at the school has to take it. Students I spoke to afterward gave a variety of majors, but none said they were comfortable speaking on the record.So later on I spoke with Sathvik Redrouthu, a sophomore who'd taken the class last year. Redrouthu, a math major, said he didn't use AI because he wanted to understand the concepts."I was interested in the class," he said, adding that mainlining the homework with AI is like "shooting yourself in the foot" for when an in-person exam comes around."I personally think that if you leave AI out, then it pushes the average student to learn properly," he said.If you're not interested in math, though, Redrouthu said you'd probably turn to AI — and you'd get away with it, until the exam at least.Ni told me that, as a professor, he can't tell whether a problem set he assigns is completed using AI. It's unlike AI-generated writing, which is usually a pretty obvious amalgamation of short sentences, em dashes, and hypophora.But math is all numbers: the specialty of AI programs.Caltech has no unified guidance for how math professors should plan around AI now. Redrouthu said that this year, some of his classes come with an auspicious caveat: "AI allowed.""Syllabuses are changing," he said.

Read next

Truman Dickerson is the Weekend News Fellow at Business Insider, based in New York City. He covers trending tech and business news. He previously reported for The Boston Globe's Express Desk. He graduated from Boston University, where he served as editor in chief of The Daily Free Press, BU's student-run newspaper.Contact him at Tdickerson@insider.com

articles.title: On Generative AI Usage in the Games Industry
articles.text:
The following manifesto was written by members of the IWGB Game Workers' Branch in collaboration with members of Game Workers Unite Ireland of the Republic of Ireland, CSVI of Spain, and the FIOM-CGIL Milan Work Council

Impact
Recommendations
Conclusion
FAQ
References

Introduction
Our Aims
We, a collective of video game unions and work councils from Europe, write this manifesto to raise awareness of the harms of generative AI (genAI) use within the video game development sector.
GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce. Left unchecked, this harm will continue to grow and impact more workers, more games, and more players, even more acutely.
Our goal is to bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce, as well as to set guidelines and standards for games industry workers, stakeholders, and regulators, suggesting actions which can be taken to reduce – and ideally eliminate – these dangers.
Scope
This manifesto discusses genAI in the context of the video game development sector. These uses include, but are not limited to:

The creation of assets included in a released game which are experienced by players – for example: art, sound, code, and dialogue assets.
The creation of materials which are used as part of the process of development but which players won’t experience when playing the released game – for example: early concept art, reference materials, pre-translations, etc.

By “genAI” we mean a specific type of AI used to generate text, pictures, videos, or music in response to limited inputs (usually just text “prompts”) using LLMs and other energy-intensive models. The wider harms of genAI won't be covered here, but they constitute additional extremely compelling reasons to resist the use of genAI. These include:

Severe harm to the environment (Zewe, 2025)
The destruction of communities (Nguyen, 2025)
The exploitation of the Global South (F.Regilme, 2025)

This document won’t go into detail about how different genAI models work, nor discuss the comparative quality of their output.
The focus of this document is on games industry workers (us!), how we are and will be impacted, and how we can resist.
The Impact of GenAI
GenAI Creates Worse Working Conditions

GenAI is both directly and indirectly replacing game industry workers.
Many game workers are being forced to use genAI, either explicitly or implicitly.
Working with genAI is less desirable, fulfilling, and educational than the same work without genAI.
Over time, working with genAI leads to worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout.
Using genAI removes a sense of ownership from workers.
GenAI is causing a marked decline in junior positions within the industry, leading to a lack of new talent.

Proponents of generative AI claim that it is a tool of empowerment for workers. For that to be true, every worker would be free to choose if, when, and how to use it. We would also need to trust that every employer would use the promised productivity improvements to benefit their workers.
In practice, this is not what we are seeing.
In many workplaces today, workers are being forced to use genAI ‘tools’, sometimes in very specific ways (Plunkett, 2025). Some companies do not explicitly impose the usage of genAI, but set expectations which cannot be reached with or without its use. Allowing the choice of usage, while also creating expectations that the worker should be able to keep pace with automated procedures, is no choice at all (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025).
When workers do use genAI, they find work more onerous than before. Many of the tasks related to genAI work are more tedious and less fulfilling, since the work becomes less about exercising the skills workers have built and invested in, and instead pivots to a plethora of small, parallel tasks which amount to supervising genAI and bug-fixing its output.
Workers using genAI have reported ‘AI brain fry’ and reduced focus (Pearl et al., 2025). Although gains to productivity are possible, these tend to be short term. Employees often initially work faster, take on larger tasks, work overtime, and ignore breaks, due to working with genAI feeling 'more like chatting' (Rangantathan & Ye, 2026). However, once this novelty declines, so does productivity, with workers reporting cognitive fatigue, burnout, and inhibited decision making.
A recent study (Shaw & Nave, 2026) showed that participants who used genAI frequently adopted results that were systematically incorrect, especially under time pressure but also in the face of incentives and feedback. The researchers were able to prove that users of genAI habitually delegate their agency and offload decision making to an external party with relative ease. They call this process ‘cognitive surrender’ (Shaw & Nave, 2026).
The use of genAI also removes a sense of ownership from workers, who become alienated from the results of their labour: the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers’ stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them.
GenAI is disproportionately used for work which would traditionally be given to junior workers, and is hence directly reducing the amount of junior positions available within the industry. This is worsening an already existing problem for newcomers to the industry, who are finding it harder than ever to find work, but it is also a loss of potential fresh perspectives, and is staggeringly short-sighted when it comes to the industry’s sustainable future.
GenAI has a profound negative impact on workers by reducing the availability and appeal of work. Games are best made by people, and people do their best when they are healthy and connected to their work, refining their skills and accumulating real experience.
GenAI Harms Relations Between Workers and Employers

GenAI is sold to employers as an alternative to workers.
GenAI often increases pressure on workers when used by employers to set policy, timescales, etc.
GenAI can be used by employers to abdicate responsibility.

GenAI’s promise to employers is to more fully automate processes, to enable them to be completed with fewer workers. This directly reduces the amount of jobs available for game workers. In some cases, workers have even been forced to train the models which then replaced them, leaving them unemployed.
GenAI interfaces are engineered to be human-like and eager-to-please, to prioritise keeping the user engaged, even if engagement comes at the cost of providing them with incorrect information. GenAI’s predisposition towards this sycophancy and lack of real-world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions (Cheng et al., 2026).
In addition, when employers engage with human-like genAI models which never tell them ‘no’, they become less receptive to criticism and pushback from other workers.
GenAI can also obfuscate and confuse employers’ accountability, in two main ways. Firstly, employers may shift their own accountability onto these platforms, blaming an error on the “tool”, rather than accepting responsibility themselves. Secondly, they may blame workers for issues which arise through the use of genAI – which the employers have mandated.
Any time genAI is used without exacting human verification, the possibility of error increases. Exacting human verification takes time, which negates the promise of genAI automation, and therefore many employers are choosing to skip this step, either directly or indirectly by imposing time constraints on workers which make detailed verification impossible. Workers are then blamed for failures in the genAI’s output.
Employers see genAI as a way of cutting labour costs, employing fewer workers than they would need to without it. GenAI companies ingratiate themselves with employers, by promising the impossible. Moreover, mistakes made by genAI are often blamed on the workers, rather than the employers mandating its use.
GenAI Appropriates the Work of Workers

GenAI models are often trained on stolen third-party data, with employers failing to credit or compensate the original creators.
Where genAI models are trained on internal data, employees/creators are likewise rarely credited or compensated.

GenAI models are mostly trained on stolen datasets, and, as stated by the owner of a genAI company, ‘impossible to create’ without stealing data (Milmo, 2024). Employers often feel entitled to automatically include their employees’ contribution into their internal dataset without consent and/or extra compensation.
This point does not require much explanation, but please do not let the relative smallness of this section undermine its importance: stealing the creations of others is wrong, creating very similar versions of those creations is wrong, and using those similar versions to generate wealth which the original creator does not share in is wrong.
GenAI does not create, it appropriates. Content output by genAI has its origins in the work of humans, who are rarely compensated for that output.
GenAI Perpetuates Discrimination

Most genAI models are trained on datasets that carry an intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities.
GenAI content averages out data used to train the AI, leading to a homogenisation of culture.

GenAI models are trained on vast swathes of historical data which is often unvetted and without context, as they aggregate large amounts of data and look for commonalities to generate a response without any direct connection to reality. The use of old data can reflect outdated opinions and values which we would be horrified at today, as well as generate middle of the road solutions.
The predominance and absence of certain types of people in historical data can also reinforce their predominance or absence in the output of genAI models today: for example, the predominance of white male doctors in historical medical literature may lead genAI models to assume that a referenced doctor is white, or to create a white male character when asked to create a doctor.
Within the games industry, this has two main types of effect: it can increase discrimination within workplaces, for example, when used in hiring practices, and it can reduce the range of representation within created media, leading to more homogenous characters and viewpoints in the games we create and play.
GenAI reproduces both historical and contemporary biases and can lead to both implicit and explicit discrimination, including but not limited to racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, etc.
GenAI Has Hidden Costs

GenAI’s output is unreliable and often incorrect.
GenAI providers obfuscate the cost of genAI, its inner workings, and its limitations.
GenAI providers aim to silo and monopolise knowledge to sell it back to corporations.

GenAI providers obscure a significant portion of their associated costs (to the environment, mental health, etc.), which impacts the ability of workers to make an informed choice on whether and how to use them (Nguyen, 2025).
GenAI platforms also disincentivise education on their limitations. Average usage of genAI goes down with increased understanding of how genAI actually works behind the scenes (Tully et al., 2025, 20).
GenAI providers sell employers a seductive image of the future, where production can be fully automated. However, in actuality, genAI platforms are gatekeeping transferable skills (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025). Once a model is trained, the ‘owner’ (usually a large conglomerate) of the trained AI has a uniquely powerful position and complete ownership over skills that were previously owned and shared by workers.
This is bad for workers, but it is also bad for employers who outsource their knowledge and skills to third-party genAI providers, as once these comp
